nutshell: Animal re-ID datasets are usually small, short time-span, and use random train/test splits that leak information between images from the same sighting. SeaTurtleID2022 introduces a 13-year, 8729-photo, 438-individual loggerhead sea turtle dataset with rich annotations (identity, timestamp, body-part segmentation masks) and proposes ecologically-motivated time-aware/open-set splits instead of random splits, then shows random splits massively overestimate real-world re-ID accuracy and proposes a head-detection + ArcFace end-to-end re-ID baseline system.
contributions: SeaTurtleID2022: the longest-spanned public wildlife re-ID dataset (8729 photos, 438 individuals, 2010-2022), with per-photo identity, encounter timestamp, and segmentation masks/bounding boxes/orientation for head, flippers, and full body.

Two ecologically-motivated dataset splits that use timestamps to prevent same-encounter leakage between train and test: a time-aware closed-set split and a time-aware open-set split (with genuinely new individuals in test/validation) - proposed as a replacement for the standard random split used elsewhere in the field.

Empirical demonstration that random splits inflate reported re-ID accuracy relative to time-aware splits by 18-54 percentage points depending on the body part/crop (Table 5), with a background/foreground-redaction ablation and Grad-CAM++ visualizations showing the random-split model is substantially relying on background cues rather than the turtle itself.

An end-to-end baseline re-ID system (Hybrid Task Cascade head detector + Swin-B ArcFace feature extractor + k-NN matching + encounter-level majority voting) reaching 86.8% accuracy, plus baseline instance-segmentation numbers (Mask R-CNN / HTC / Mask2Former x ResNet50/Swin-B) for head/turtle/flipper masks.
deficiencies: The paper's own body-parts ablation (Table 5) shows full-image accuracy (17.1% time-aware) is dramatically worse than head-crop accuracy (69.2%) even before considering the random-vs-time-aware gap - yet the central random-split-inflation demonstration (Tables 5 and 6, Fig. 7) is built primarily around full-image inputs, the worst-performing crop by their own numbers, rather than the head crops the paper itself recommends as most informative.

The 'Note' callout explicitly states the open-set split 'should be preferred... over the closed-set problem' for evaluation, but every baseline result reported in the main text (Tables 4-7, the 86.8% end-to-end system) uses only the closed-set split - the open-set split is described and given dataset statistics (Table 3) but never actually benchmarked anywhere in the paper.

Table 4 shows the classical local-descriptor methods actually used by working conservation researchers in the wild (Wild ID, Hotspotter - both cited as the field's most popular tools) perform far worse than deep metric learning on this dataset (SIFT 8.4%, Superpoint 20.2% vs. ArcFace 34.7%), a gap the paper doesn't discuss despite it being directly relevant to whether the benchmark reflects tools conservationists currently deploy.

The headline 86.8% end-to-end system accuracy (Sec. 5, using automatic HTC head detection) is not directly reconciled against the 88.4% encounter-level head accuracy reported elsewhere (Table 5, apparently using pre-cropped heads) - the ~1.6-point gap presumably reflects head-detector error, but the paper doesn't walk through this, leaving the actual detection-stage error rate unquantified.
notable: The paper's finding that turtle heads massively outperform other body parts for re-ID (+34.5 absolute accuracy points over full body) directly contradicts a specific prior study (Mills et al., cited as ref [34]) that found flipper scales more accurate than head scales for sea turtle photo-ID - the paper notes the contradiction in one sentence ('In contrast to the findings of [34]...') without further investigation into why the two studies disagree, which would be useful context for anyone building on either result. Also notable: all segmentation-mask annotations were produced semi-automatically using Meta's Segment Anything Model (SAM) inside CVAT rather than fully manually - a practical, reusable annotation pipeline for other wildlife re-ID dataset efforts.

results.setting: automatic HTC head detection + Swin-B ArcFace + k-NN + encounter majority vote
Mask2Former + Swin-B backbone, closed-set split, avg over head/turtle/flippers
